title: The 14-Inch Hole That Swallowed a Lake
description: In 1980, a simple drilling error dissolved a salt mine beneath Lake Peigneur, swallowing an entire lake and reversing the flow of the Gulf of Mexico. Did you know about this insane geological disaster?
script:
It sounds like a glitch in the fundamental laws of nature: a single 14-inch drill bit accidentally punctures the bottom of a shallow lake, triggering an apocalyptic chain reaction that swallows 3.5 billion gallons of water, eleven barges, a tugboat, and fifty-five acres of surrounding land in a matter of hours. Yet on November 20, 1980, this exact scenario played out at Lake Peigneur in Iberia Parish, Louisiana, resulting in one of the most incredible human-made geological disasters in history.

The setup was a catastrophic collision of industrial interests. Texaco was operating a contract oil rig on the surface of the shallow, ten-foot-deep freshwater lake. Unbeknownst to the drill crew—due to a fatal miscalculation in map coordinate projections—their target lay directly above the sprawling, multi-level cavern network of the Diamond Crystal Salt Mine, which had been actively excavated 1,300 feet underground for decades.

When Texaco’s 14-inch bit pierced the roof of a salt mine shaft, water began to seep down the borehole. What the engineers overlooked was the simple chemistry of salt. As freshwater rushed into the opening, it rapidly dissolved the solid halite pillars supporting the mine walls. Within minutes, the 14-inch hole dilated into a gaping subterranean abyss.

The resulting vortex created a terrifying whirlpool that swallowed the 4,500-ton oil rig, eleven barges loaded with soil, a tugboat, a mobile home, and fifty-five acres of the adjacent Rip Van Winkle Gardens. Miraculously, despite the sudden collapse, all fifty-five miners underground and the three oil rig workers escaped alive, saved by early evacuation warnings and lucky timing.

The ultimate payoff was a complete rewrite of local geography. The lake drained so violently that it created a massive hydraulic vacuum, temporarily reversing the flow of the Delcambre Canal. Saltwater from the Gulf of Mexico rushed inland to fill the void, creating Louisiana's tallest waterfall at 150 feet as the empty mine pit filled. In just two days, Lake Peigneur was permanently transformed from a shallow freshwater lake into a 1,300-foot-deep saltwater bay.

chosen_topic: In 1980, an oil rig accidentally drilled a 14-inch hole into an underground salt mine beneath Lake Peigneur, creating a massive whirlpool that swallowed the entire 1,300-acre lake, 11 barges, and surrounding land in hours. Miraculously, all 55 workers escaped alive before the drainage temporarily reversed the flow of the Gulf of Mexico to fill the giant crater.
